871: Tax refund/deficiency: whether losses claimed by RRF were attributable to partnership item and whether the IRS limitations period was suspended by the 2005 FPAA, so assessment against indirect partner was timely and proper

We hold the Court of Federal Claims correctly determined that the losses claimed on Ms. Zimmerman's 2001 tax return are "attributable to" the loss claimed in RRF's 2000 tax return, the limitations period for which was suspended by the 2005 FPAA.
872: Whether Tiger was a bona fide partner in RRF and the contribution of CLNs was a valid partnership contribution (sham transaction, economic substance doctrine)
Because there was no bona fide partnership between RRF and Tiger, we hold that the Court of Federal Claims did not err.
873: Reasonable cause exception to the 40% accuracy-related penalty under I.R.C. 6664(c)(1) based on reliance on professional tax advice
We agree with the Court of Federal Claims that RRF cannot meet its burden.
1062: Federal tax refund claims for tax years 2004, 2009, 2011, 2012 and 2013 dismissed as not timely or not properly brought.
We agree with the Court of Federal Claims that Ms. Langley’s refund claims were not timely filed.
1245: Whether Nacchio's criminal forfeiture payment is deductible as a loss under I.R.C. § 165 or is barred as a fine or similar penalty under § 162(f) and the frustration-of-public-policy doctrine; the court held it nondeductible and reversed the trial court.
For all of these reasons, we hold that the trial court erred in ruling that Nacchio may deduct his forfeiture under § 165.
1246: Whether the forfeiture is deductible as an ordinary and necessary business expense under I.R.C. § 162(a); the court affirmed that § 162(f) bars the deduction.
Because § 162(f) also applies to loss deductions under § 162(a), we affirm the trial court's ruling that Nacchio cannot deduct his forfeiture under § 162 for the reasons articulated in Section A.
1247: Whether Nacchio may seek special tax relief under I.R.C. § 1341, which requires an independent deduction under another section; the court held he may not.

Because the parties do not dispute that deductibility under another provision of the tax code is a prerequisite to deductibility under § 1341, we further hold that Nacchio also may not seek special tax relief under § 1341.
1285: Tax refund: whether the Bx payments from Barclays are income to BB&T under Old Colony rather than a tax rebate reducing creditable foreign taxes. Court rejected the government's rebate characterization.
We therefore conclude that the Bx payments should not be characterized as tax effects. Pursuant to Old Colony and its progeny, the Bx payments are income to BB&T.
1286: Tax refund: whether the STARS Trust transaction lacked economic substance and a bona fide business purpose, so its foreign tax credits must be disregarded. Court sustained the trial court's finding.
We therefore sustain the trial court's finding that the STARS Trust lacked a bona fide business purpose. The tax consequences of the STARS Trust accordingly must be disregarded.
1287: Tax refund: whether the STARS Loan had economic substance so that BB&T may deduct interest paid on the $1.5 billion Loan. Court reversed the trial court and allowed the deductions.
Accordingly, we hold that the Loan portion of the transaction satisfies the economic substance test and that BB&T is entitled to claim interest deductions for the interest it paid on the Loan.
1288: Accuracy-related penalties under section 6662: whether BB&T had reasonable cause and acted in good faith in relying on Sidley and PwC advice. Court upheld the penalties.
We conclude that the trial court did not err in imposing accuracy-related penalties on BB&T.
1758: Tax refund suit: whether the FICA hospital insurance tax on nonqualified deferred compensation, calculated under Treasury's present-value regulation (26 C.F.R. § 31.3121(v)(2)-1(c)(2)(ii)), was refundable; court held the regulation satisfies Chevron and State Farm, so no refund.
This is neither arbitrary nor capricious.
1801: Tax refund suit for Federal Communications Excise Tax; 8x8 as collector failed to meet I.R.C. § 6415(a) and did not bear the economic burden of the tax, so no refund.
We agree with the Court of Federal Claims that 8x8 is a collector of the FCET and, as a collector, 8x8 has failed to fulfill the necessary requirements of I.R.C. § 6415(a).
1821: Tax refund: interpretation of Treas. Reg. § 1.165-1(d)(3) as a single test asking when no reasonable prospect of recovery remains, rejecting the Claims Court's separate, stricter 'reasonable certainty' standard for years after discovery of a theft loss.
We agree with the Adkinses’ interpretation of the regulation.
1822: Tax refund: the Claims Court erred by treating abandonment of the pending arbitration claim as a prerequisite to showing reasonable certainty of no recovery; remanded for holistic analysis of all facts and circumstances.
Once again, we find the Adkinses’ argument persuasive, and hold that the Claims Court so erred.
1839: Tax refund suit: whether 26 U.S.C. § 461(h) applies to determine when and whether an accrual-method taxpayer incurs assumed nuclear decommissioning liabilities for purposes of calculating the basis of acquired nuclear power plants.

We therefore agree with the Claims Court and conclude that § 461(h) is applicable in determining when and whether an accrual method taxpayer, such as AmerGen, incurs nuclear decommissioning liabilities for purposes of calculating the basis of acquired nuclear power plants and associated assets.
1840: Tax refund suit: whether economic performance of the assumed decommissioning liabilities occurred at purchase under § 461(h)(2)(A)(ii), or instead under § 461(h)(2)(B) when decommissioning occurs, so the liabilities were not includable in basis for 2001-2003.
Under § 461(h), the economic performance of AmerGen's decommissioning liabilities occurs when AmerGen actually decommissions its nuclear power plants.
1854: Tax refund interest netting under I.R.C. § 6621(d) for Situation One: whether a post-merger surviving corporation may net an underpayment against a premerger overpayment made by a separate predecessor corporation (same taxpayer requirement not met).
We hold that Wells Fargo may not net interest in Situation One.
1855: Tax refund interest netting under I.R.C. § 6621(d) for Situation Three: whether an acquired corporation's premerger overpayment and the post-merger surviving corporation's underpayment satisfy the same taxpayer requirement, so interest may be netted.

we hold that an acquired corporation that makes an overpayment before a merger is the "same taxpayer" for the purposes of § 6621(d) as the post-merger surviving entity that has absorbed the acquired corporation.
2843: Tax refund: whether the Sandovals withdrew their Form 4549 waiver of notice of deficiency, so that the 2003 and 2004 assessments were invalid. Court held no withdrawal was proven and the refund was properly denied.
Without proof of withdrawal of the waiver, the IRS properly denied the Sandovals' refund request as a matter of law.
2845: Tax refund: whether the 2008 remittances were deposits or tax payments, including the equitable estoppel argument against applying Revenue Procedure 2005-18. Court held they were tax payments and no affirmative misconduct was shown.
They were tax payments, not deposits.
3125: Tax refund: whether MassMutual and ConnMutual could deduct guaranteed policyholder dividends in the year the dividends were fixed, i.e., the all-events test and the recurring item exception, resulting in a refund entitlement

Because we find that MassMutual's and ConnMutual's policyholder dividends were fixed in the year the dividends were announced, that the dividends in question are premium adjustments, and that premium adjustments are rebates, thereby satisfying the recurring item exception, we affirm.
3279: Federal tax refund suit: whether Albemarle's contested foreign tax liability accrued in the year of origin for foreign tax credit purposes, so that the government's position on the credit and refund prevails.
we reject Albemarle's interpretation of the statutory phrase "actually paid or accrued."
3338: Tax refund suit: whether the settlement payment received for withdrawing employment-discrimination/whistleblower claims was capital gain from a sale or exchange of goodwill, so as to qualify for capital-gain treatment rather than ordinary income
Therefore, the Court of Federal Claims correctly granted summary judgment for the government.
3418: Tax refund suit: amended 2005 refund claim held time-barred under IRC § 6511(a); the four-year period in Treas. Reg. § 301.6511(g)-1 held inapplicable.
Treas. Reg. § 301.6511(g)-1(a) does not apply, and the McNaughtons can point to no other statutory provision providing for a period of limitation longer than three years.
3727: Tax refund jurisdiction: whether the taxpayer's suit was a tax refund suit within Claims Court jurisdiction; no refund claim was shown to the IRS.
There is no jurisdiction over this action as a tax refund suit.
4085: Tax refund suit under 28 U.S.C. § 1346(a)(1): claimant must show payment of assessed tax and a timely refund claim; not shown here.

to invoke the court's jurisdiction over a tax refund claim a claimant must show that he paid the assessed tax prior to filing his complaint and that he filed a timely claim for a tax refund with the IRS.
4880: Tax refund suit: whether Appellants overpaid their 2006 and 2007 income taxes so as to be entitled to return of levied funds; court held no overpayment shown and affirmed summary judgment for the government.
Because Appellants have not met their burden to demonstrate an overpayment of income taxes, we affirm.
4993: Tax refunds: whether nonprofit, state-incorporated taxpayers are 'corporations' under 26 U.S.C. § 6621(a)(1), so that the lower corporate overpayment interest rate applies. The court held they are corporations and the government's reading prevails.
Thus, the ordinary meaning of the word “corporation” extends to nonprofit entities.
5016: Tax refund: whether the Claims Court applied the correct legal framework, including the taxpayer's burden to prove cost basis to a reasonable degree of certainty and the refusal to make a best-guess valuation.
We therefore conclude that the Claims Court did not apply an incorrect legal framework.
5017: Tax refund: WMI's failure to establish cost basis in the supervisory-merger RAP rights, found not clearly erroneous.
Because the court's findings are not clearly erroneous, we affirm the court's ruling.
5018: Tax refund: WMI's failure to establish cost basis in the supervisory-merger branching rights, found not clearly erroneous.
Because the court's findings are not clearly erroneous, we affirm the court's ruling.
5019: Tax refund: whether the 1988 Bowery assistance exchange was a realization event triggering gain and whether it qualified as a like-kind exchange under section 1031 deferring recognition.
We agree with the Claims Court that Bowery's 1988 receipt of an assistance package was a realization event, and we therefore affirm the court's ruling.
5020: Tax refund suit: Court of Federal Claims found Norman's 2007 FBAR violation willful and upheld the $803,530 penalty; clear-error review of willfulness finding.
we cannot say that the Court of Federal Claims clearly erred in finding that Ms. Norman willfully violated the FBAR requirement.
5021: Whether the 2004 amendment to 31 U.S.C. § 5321 superseded the 1987 Treasury regulation capping willful FBAR penalties at $100,000, limiting the penalty amount in the tax refund suit.
we find that the 2004 amendment to 31 U.S.C. § 5321 rendered void the 1987 regulation capping penalties for willful violations of § 5314 at $100,000.
5051: Tax refund suit: whether Alternative Carbon sold the feedstock/diesel alternative fuel mixture under 26 U.S.C. § 6426(e), including application of the economic substance doctrine, so that it was entitled to the alternative fuel mixture credits. Court held no sale occurred.
Accordingly, we agree with the Claims Court that the government was entitled to summary judgment.
5052: Penalties under 26 U.S.C. § 6675(a): whether Alternative Carbon had reasonable cause for claiming the credits, so as to avoid the excessive-claim penalties. Court held no reasonable cause was shown.
we agree with the Claims Court that Alternative Carbon cannot establish that it had reasonable cause to claim the credits based on Sanderson's advice or otherwise.
5246: Tax refund suit jurisdiction: Claims Court dismissed complaint for lack of tax refund jurisdiction because plaintiff did not allege prepayment of the tax deficiency; affirmed.
There is no jurisdiction over this action as a tax refund suit.
5566: Federal tax refund suit for overpaid large corporate underpayment interest; the court held the refund claims barred, so the taxpayer's refund suit failed for the government.
GMI's refund claims based on alleged IRS computational errors were brought well after the period established by the applicable statute of limitations had run.
5641: Tax refund/interest netting under 26 U.S.C. § 6621(d): whether Ford and its FSC subsidiary were the 'same taxpayer' for interest netting; court held they were not the same taxpayer, affirming judgment for the government.
Thus, we affirm the trial court's grant of the government's motion for summary judgment.
5654: Tax refund suit: taxpayer failed to show full payment of disputed taxes and failed to seek refund from IRS before suing
Ms. Pekrul has not shown that either prerequisite was met.
6026: Whether IRC § 3102(b) is a money-mandating source of substantive law supporting Tucker Act jurisdiction over the hospital's indemnity claim for FICA refund-related settlement payments (tax refund suit context)
we hold that § 3102(b) is money-mandating and that the Court of Federal Claims erred in concluding that it lacked subject matter jurisdiction over the Hospital's Complaint.
6044: Merits of the 2016-2018 tax refund claims: whether Walby was a non-citizen not subject to federal income tax; the court held she is a U.S. citizen and a resident for tax purposes, so the claims fail.
Walby, born in Michigan to parents who were not foreign diplomats and themselves were born in the United States, provides no basis on which she falls outside that language.
6288: Tax refund: whether the Adkinses were entitled to a theft loss deduction under 26 U.S.C. § 165(e) and Treas. Reg. § 1.165-1(d), i.e., whether they lacked a reasonable prospect of recovery in 2004. The court held the Claims Court misapplied an 'unknowable' standard and clearly erred in finding no showing of no reasonable prospect of recovery.

we reverse the Claims Court's conclusion that the Adkinses failed to show that, as of 2004, they lacked a reasonable prospect of recovery for the losses they incurred by virtue of the substantial fraud perpetuated upon them.
6323: Tax refund suit: whether the alcohol fuel mixture credit under 26 U.S.C. 6426 reduces gasoline excise-tax liability under 4081 before any remaining credit is paid as a tax-free direct payment under 6427(e); court held the credit must first offset excise tax, so the refund claim fails.
we conclude that the § 6426(a) Mixture Credit is a reduction of § 4081 excise-tax liability, with any credit amount exceeding said excise-tax liability to be paid to the taxpayer under § 6427(e).
6674: Tax refund: whether the excess amount of a New York brownfield redevelopment tax credit paid in cash to the taxpayers is federally taxable gross income, rejecting their return-of-capital and common-law inducement arguments.

The excess amount of the brownfield redevelopment tax credit received by the Ginsburgs in 2013 is taxable gross income because it is an undeniable accession to wealth over which the Ginsburgs have complete dominion and control.
6717: Tax refund suit under 28 U.S.C. § 1346(a)(1) failed because taxes were not shown to be fully paid and no refund was sought from the IRS.
Mr. Pekrul has not shown that either prerequisite was met.
6819: Tax refund for tax year 2010 barred by the three-year lookback of I.R.C. § 6511(b)(2)(A).
Because the record reflects that the credits were deemed to have been paid more than three years before Appellants filed a refund claim, the refund claim is barred by § 6511.
7336: Tax refund suit: whether section 101(d) of the AJCA provides transitional tax relief for extraterritorial income recognized after 2006 from a 2006 transaction

we conclude that section 101(d) unambiguously provides transitional relief for all extraterritorial income received from transactions entered into in 2005 and 2006, even if that income is received in later years.
7416: Tax refund: mitigation provisions (§§ 1311-1314) do not allow the Stephenses to recover time-barred refunds for 1995-1997, so the refund claim fails for the government.
Accordingly, the Claims Court's order granting the Government's motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction is AFFIRMED
7558: Tax refund: whether Kimble's failure to file an FBAR was a willful violation under 31 U.S.C. § 5321(a)(5), based on reckless disregard and constructive knowledge.
Under these facts, it was not clear error for the Court of Federal Claims to hold that she committed a willful violation.
7559: Tax refund: whether the IRS abused its discretion in assessing the maximum 50% civil penalty under § 5321(a)(5)(C), including the § 1010.820 regulation question and the IRS mitigation guidelines.
We now affirm the Court of Federal Claims' holding that the IRS did not abuse its discretion in assessing the statutory maximum civil penalty of 50% of the bank account's value.
8152: Tax refund suit: whether a butane-gasoline mixture qualifies for the alternative fuel mixture credit under 26 U.S.C. § 6426(e), i.e., whether butane is an alternative fuel; court held butane is a taxable fuel and not an alternative fuel, so no refund.

Because the Claims Court correctly concluded that butane is not an "alternative fuel" for purposes of § 6426, Philadelphia Energy's mixture of butane with gasoline does not qualify for the alternative fuel mixture credit.
8574: Tax refund suit barred because the taxpayer did not pay the assessed taxes in full or file a refund claim
we see no error in the Claims Court's findings that Mr. Schroeder did not pre-pay his back taxes or file any refund claims.
8663: Tax refund suit jurisdiction: whether plaintiff satisfied the full payment rule / divisibility exception by a $100 token payment toward the §6672 penalty; court held not satisfied and dismissed for lack of jurisdiction
We therefore agree with the Claims Court's ultimate conclusion that Mr. Bishay did not establish subject matter jurisdiction over his tax refund action.
8913: Tax refunds: whether Roman was a 'taxpayer' entitled to sue for a refund of taxes assessed against another person (his ex-wife).
In short, Mr. Roman was not a "taxpayer" as required by 28 U.S.C. § 1346(a)(1) because he was not the person against whom the tax liability was assessed.
9304: Federal tax refund suit for 1997 tax year; dismissed because the refund claim was not timely filed with the IRS under 26 U.S.C. § 6511(a).

Because their request fell well outside the time limits set forth in 26 U.S.C. § 6511(a), the Court of Federal Claims correctly dismissed this action for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 7422(a).
9565: Tax refund merits: the Browns' refund claims were not duly filed under 26 U.S.C. 7422(a) because they were unsigned and unverified by the taxpayers and lacked powers of attorney.
we agree with the Claims Court's conclusion that the Browns did not 'duly file' their refund claim in accordance with § 7422(a).
9566: Whether the IRS waived the taxpayer signature and verification requirements under Angelus Milling; the court held the waiver doctrine did not apply.
the Browns are incorrect to presume that the signature and verification requirements were waived.
9733: Tax refund suit: whether the taxpayer could recover refunds for 2013 and 2014 given the defective and untimely 2020 Forms 1040X; the court affirmed dismissal for the government.
For the reasons we have given, however, we conclude that the doctrine does not apply here. It follows that the Claims Court properly dismissed the present refund action.
9982: Tax refund under 26 U.S.C. § 1341: appellants failed to plead an unrestricted right to funds obtained by fraud and failed to tether the deduction to another Code section, so the refund claim fails as a matter of law.

we hold that the Court of Federal Claims properly dismissed the case because the appellants (1) did not have an unrestricted right to funds acquired by fraud as a matter of law, foreclosing their ability to plead a claim under § 1341
10160: Federal tax refund suit for FICA taxes paid up front on deferred compensation; refund claims failed, so the refund suit was dismissed in the government's favor.
For the reasons provided below, we affirm the decisions of the Claims Court.
10174: Federal tax refund suit for 2003 tax year; court affirmed dismissal because taxpayer failed to establish a timely refund claim, a prerequisite to the refund action.
We hold that Appellant failed to establish the timely filing of a 2003 refund claim, which is a prerequisite for bringing his tax refund action.
10687: Federal tax refund suit: whether the $22.5 million 2011 loss allocated to GSS was properly disallowed under 26 U.S.C. § 707(b)(1) via the step transaction doctrine; Claims Court applied a hybrid step-transaction/economic-substance standard, so the court vacated and remanded without deciding the merits.
Because we conclude that the Claims Court erred by applying an incorrect legal standard to reach its decision, we vacate the judgment and remand for a determination under the correct legal standard.
11427: Tax refund: validity and enforceability of the 2015-2017 IRS Closing Agreement under I.R.C. § 7121, including whether the IRS had authority to enter it, barring the § 911 exclusion; judgment for the government on the 2017 refund claim.
We agree with the government that the Closing Agreement was valid and enforceable.
11428: Tax refund: whether the Closing Agreement could be rescinded under I.R.C. § 7121(b) for fraud, malfeasance, or misrepresentation of material fact; rescission rejected.
Mr. Baney failed to prove that any of these bases for rescission are present here.
11429: Tax refund: whether the Closing Agreement is unenforceable because Ms. Baney did not sign it; held that Mr. Baney, who signed, is bound.
The only income involved here is Mr. Baney's income and there is no dispute that Mr. Baney duly executed the agreement. He, therefore, is bound by it.
11536: Tax refund suit: the Federal Circuit held that the power-of-attorney 'accompany' requirement of 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(e) is regulatory rather than statutory and therefore waivable by the IRS, vacating the dismissal of the refund complaint for failure to duly file.
We conclude that 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(e)'s requirement that "a power of attorney must accompany the claim" is regulatory and not statutory.
12222: Tax refund: whether the Convention's paragraph 2(a) credit clause, subject to the U.S. Law Limitation, allows a foreign tax credit against the NIIT; Federal Circuit agreed with the Court of Federal Claims that no offset is allowed.

we agree with the Court of Federal Claims and reject the Christensens’ contention that the paragraph 2(a) Credit Clause of the Convention entitles them to a foreign tax credit that may be used to offset the NIIT owed to the IRS.
12223: Tax refund: whether the U.S. Law Limitation applies to the paragraph 2(b) credit clause, so that the NIIT cannot be offset by a French-tax credit; Federal Circuit held the limitation applies and reversed the Court of Federal Claims.
For this, as well as the other reasons we have given, we hold that the U.S. Law Limitation applies to the paragraph 2(b) Credit Clause.
12596: Tax refund suit dismissed under Rule 12(b)(6) as barred by claim preclusion from prior district court judgment enforcing tax and penalty liens
We disagree with her arguments on all three elements.
12654: Whether Actavis's Hatch-Waxman litigation expenses were deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC 162 rather than capital expenditures under IRC 263 and Treas. Reg. 1.263(a)-4, so that Actavis was entitled to a tax refund.

Because the costs incurred in defending Hatch-Waxman litigation are deductible as business expenses, whether considered under the 'origin of the claim' standard or C.F.R. § 1.263, we affirm the Court of Federal Claims' grant of summary judgment for Actavis and against the government.
12775: Tax refund: whether the 1980 U.S.-Canada Convention (Article XXIV) creates a foreign tax credit that can offset the U.S. net investment income tax (NIIT) under Code § 1411, entitling the taxpayer to a refund. The court held the Code and Convention preclude the credit, so the government prevails.

we agree with the government: the Code does not allow Bruyea to apply a foreign tax credit for the taxes he paid to Canada (on the income he realized for his sale of property in Canada) as an offset to the net investment income tax he owes the U.S. under Code § 1411.
13029: Federal income tax refund claims for 2019 and 2022 dismissed because the refund claims were not duly filed with the IRS (26 U.S.C. § 7422(a); 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1)).
13059: Transferee liability under 26 U.S.C. 6901 and NY UFCA 273: collapsing the stock sale and asset sales and finding the Dillon trusts had constructive knowledge of the fraudulent scheme

we see no error in the Court of Federal Claims' finding that the Dillon trusts had constructive knowledge of the entire fraudulent scheme and resulting decision to collapse the transactions in order to assign transferee liability to them.
13060: Whether the transferee-liability cap in NY UFCA 278(2) applies, given that constructive fraud under 273 precludes a lack of actual fraudulent intent
the fact that the transactions were collapsed and transferee liability assessed under § 273 does not entitle the Dillon trusts to use of the cap on liability in § 278(2).
13061: Whether transferees are liable for the transferor's gross valuation misstatement penalty and pre-notice interest under federal law
we see no error in the Court of Federal Claims' decision to include the penalties owed by HSHC in the Dillon trusts' transferee liability.
13968: Tax refund under I.R.C. § 7422: the complaint failed to state a refund claim because the May 2022 letters were not a duly filed, adequate refund claim (substantial variance, waiver and informal claim doctrines did not save it).
We therefore affirm the dismissal of the complaint to the extent it seeks a tax refund.
14156: Tax refund merits: challenge to 26 U.S.C. § 3121(v)(2) special timing rule for FICA tax on deferred compensation; court held the statute's application to pilots' deferred benefits is permissible and affirmed dismissal for failure to state a claim.

The short answer to that contention is that the special timing rule of 26 U.S.C. § 3121(v)(2) creates a statutory exception to the general rule of 26 U.S.C. § 3102, something that Congress is entitled to do and clearly did.
14638: Tax refund suit: FICA refund claims for taxes paid under the special timing rule of 26 U.S.C. 3121(v)(2) were barred; the court rejected the pilots' argument that the tax was unlawful because the benefits were not yet received.
Congress is entitled to adopt different ways of defining wages in different circumstances.
14962: Tax refund claim: Noll did not make full payment, file a timely refund claim with the IRS, or file a timely refund suit, so the refund claim failed.
Mr. Noll has done none of this, and in fact, continues to assert that he is not subject to federal income tax.
